title: 2021 AMC 12B Problem 22
statement:
Arjun and Beth play a game in which they take turns removing one brick or two adjacent bricks from one “wall” among a set of several walls of bricks, with gaps possibly creating new walls. The walls are one brick tall. For example, a set of walls of sizes \(4\) and \(2\) can be changed into any of the following by one move: \((3,2),\) \(\ (2,1,2),\) \(\ (4),\) \(\ (4,1),\) \(\ (2,2),\) or \((1,1,2).\)

Arjun plays first, and the player who removes the last brick wins. For which starting configuration is there a strategy that guarantees a win for Beth?

solutions.text:
Treat each wall as a Nim-like heap with a Grundy value. A move removes \(1\) or \(2\) adjacent bricks, possibly splitting a wall into lengths \(a,b.\) Thus \(g(n)\) is the mex of \(g(a)\oplus g(b)\) over \(a+b=n-1\) or \(a+b=n-2.\)

Starting with \(g(0)=0,\) this recurrence gives \(g(1),g(2),\ldots,g(6)\) equal to \(1,2,3,1,4,3,\) respectively.

The second player Beth wins exactly when the XOR of the walls’ Grundy values is \(0.\) Checking each option, only \((6,2,1)\) gives \(g(6)\oplus g(2)\oplus g(1)\) \(=3\oplus 2\oplus 1=0.\)

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: Compute the Grundy value of a single wall of length \(n,\) where a move removes \(1\) or \(2\) adjacent bricks and may split the wall
Beth (the second player) wins exactly when the XOR of the walls’ Grundy values is \(0\)
